strengths: The paper proposes a novel occupancy-centric framework for robot video generation that leverages 4D semantic occupancy as a fine-grained intermediate representation for controllable video synthesis. This is a reasonable and useful idea that addresses the coarse alignment problem of high-level action/task prompts.

The work is comprehensive, with three coordinated components (single-view ORV, ORV-MV for multiview, ORV-S2R for sim-to-real) and a substantial dataset curation pipeline that uses VLMs, GroundingDINO, SAM2, Monst3R and NKSR to construct pseudo-occupancy labels from existing robot datasets.

Quantitative results in Table 2 show consistent improvements over CogVideoX, AVID, HMA and IRASim across three datasets (BridgeV2, Droid, RT-1) on PSNR, SSIM, FID and FVD, which is meaningful evidence of generation quality improvements.

The ablation studies (Tables 3 and 4) are informative, showing that adding depth and semantic occupancy conditions substantially improves PSNR (from ~25.6 to ~28.3), and that the pretrained CogVideoX backbone is important for FID/FVD.

The paper is generally well written and includes extensive supplementary material with implementation details, hyperparameters, and additional qualitative examples, supporting reproducibility (code/model said to be publicly available).
weaknesses: The central motivation is 'precise controllability' and 'fine-grained' control, but the evaluation relies almost entirely on pixel-reconstruction metrics (PSNR/SSIM/FID/FVD). There is no direct quantitative measure of control precision (e.g., end-effector/object pose alignment, action-following error), which weakens the core claim.

The claimed 'sim-to-real transfer' (ORV-S2R) is supported only by a single qualitative example (Figure 7) with no quantitative evaluation, despite being a prominent contribution in the abstract and introduction.

The multiview generation (ORV-MV) is also evaluated only qualitatively (Figure 8, Figure I). No quantitative cross-view consistency metric is reported, and the lighting/color inconsistency is acknowledged but not measured.

The paper repeatedly argues the approach benefits 'downstream robotic learning tasks,' yet no downstream task (e.g., policy learning or imitation learning using the generated data) is evaluated, so this important claim is left unvalidated.

The comparison set is limited: among the baselines only IRASim is a directly comparable robot-video generation method; comparisons with other concurrent works (UniSim, EnerVerse, TesserAct, RoboMaster) are absent, and the text-to-video CogVideoX baseline is a comparatively weak control-conditioned reference.

The occupancy representation is reconstructed from monocular video via Monst3R + NKSR, which can be noisy and unreliable; the quality/accuracy of the pseudo-occupancy ground truth is not itself evaluated, yet it is the central intermediate representation driving the method.

The dataset curation pipeline is expensive and engineering-heavy (VLM captioning, GroundingDINO, SAM2, Monst3R, NKSR, K-means over ~150K captions, 8TB disk for BridgeV2 alone); the practical scalability of the pipeline to new datasets is not discussed quantitatively.

Key architectural and implementation details (e.g., the exact fusion of multiple visual conditions, positional encodings, 3D VAE frame padding) are deferred almost entirely to the supplementary, making the main paper harder to assess on its own.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem framing: the paper correctly identifies that prior action- or text-conditioned robot video generators (IRASim, RoboMaster, UniSim, EnerVerse, TesserAct) use globally coarse control signals that align poorly with low-level pixel dynamics, and proposes 4D semantic occupancy as a fine-grained spatial-temporal conditioning signal. The idea is sensible and the pipeline is coherent.

Strong and consistent quantitative results across three real datasets. Table 2 shows ORV substantially outperforming all baselines on BridgeV2 (PSNR 28.258 vs. IRASim 25.276 / HMA 23.636; FVD 16.525 vs. 20.910 / 67.096), Droid, and RT-1, with gains that are large enough to be meaningful rather than marginal.

The dataset curation pipeline (Figure 3) is a substantial and reusable engineering contribution: VLM captioning + K-means over ~150K objects to build a dataset-level label set, Grounding DINO + SAM2 for temporally consistent instance masks, Monst3R + NKSR for dense geometry, and Gaussian-based rendering with depth-adaptive scaling (σ = k·d̂^α). Details (voxel size, spatial extents, α/β) are given in Sec. E.1.

Ablations substantiate the core design. Table 3 isolates the effect of conditioning: base (action-only) 25.631 PSNR → full condition 28.258, with depth and semantics both contributing, and rendering-based conditions performing comparably to reconstruction-based ones (relevant for sim-to-real). Table 4 supports the pretraining choice (FID 3.821 vs. 9.357 from scratch). Figure F provides per-sample improvement curves, and Figures E/G qualitatively demonstrate failure cases of the unconditioned model.

Methodological details are generally well specified (action conditioning via chunk-level injection into the Vision Expert AdaLN, a shallow visual-embedding MLP for 2D condition maps, cross-view attention for ORV-MV), and the supplementary provides hyperparameters (Table 5), preprocessing settings (Table 6), and compute cost (8×H100, ~35 GPU-hours per 30K steps), which supports reproducibility.
The extensions (ORV-MV for multi-view consistency and ORV-S2R for sim-to-real) are natural and demonstrated with qualitative examples, and limitations are openly discussed in Sec. G.
weaknesses: The occupancy representation that the entire method depends on is never quantitatively validated. The 4D semantic occupancy is pseudo-ground-truth derived from Monst3R/NKSR/VLM/DINO/SAM2 (Sec. 3.1), and there is no evaluation of its geometric or semantic accuracy (e.g., against any reference, or an ablation on occupancy noise/quality). Since conditioning errors propagate directly into the generated video, the reader cannot tell how much of the gain comes from accurate occupancy versus simply supplying extra input channels. This is a material gap for a paper whose central claim is 'occupancy-centric'.

No downstream robot learning evaluation, despite this being the stated motivation. The abstract and intro repeatedly claim usefulness for policy/imitation learning and 'downstream robotic learning tasks,' but no policy is trained on the generated data and no task success rates are reported. The practical usefulness claim therefore remains unvalidated.

Sim-to-real transfer (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 7) is evaluated qualitatively only. No quantitative metric (visual fidelity, task success, or comparison against the simulator's rendering) is given. Moreover, the setting is closer to re-rendering simulated geometry with real-world appearance using a model trained on real data—the dynamics come from the simulator and the appearance from the generative prior—so the 'sim-to-real' framing is somewhat stronger than what is demonstrated.

Multi-view generation (Sec. 4.2, Fig. 8) is also qualitative only. No quantitative cross-view consistency metric and no multi-view baselines are provided. Figure I hints that reference-view-only conditioning degrades under side views, but this is not quantified.

The baseline set is limited (CogVideoX, AVID, HMA, IRASim). Recent robot world-model generators mentioned in related work (e.g., RoboMaster, UniSim, EnerVerse, TesserAct) are not compared, and the paper does not establish that the baselines were trained/finetuned under comparable data and compute budgets, which is important for a fair PSNR/FVD comparison.

The action conditioning only encodes end-effector poses; the authors themselves note (Sec. G) that this is insufficient for articulated arms such as the Google robot used in Droid, yet Droid results are reported without addressing how much this limits control precision on that dataset. The claim of 'more precise controllability' is therefore only indirectly supported.

Metric choice is misaligned with the central claim. PSNR/SSIM/FID/FVD measure appearance fidelity, not control precision or physical plausibility. The paper asserts improved motion accuracy (Sec. 4.1, Table 3 discussion) without reporting an action-following/control error metric.

Minor presentation issues: the main text refers to 'Table 7' for the pretraining ablation while the table is labeled Table 4; the abstract truncates 'Demo, Code & Model:' without a visible link; several figures are low-resolution and rely on 'better to zoom in.'

strengths: The central idea—using 4D semantic occupancy as a spatially and temporally aligned intermediate representation to condition robot video generation—is well motivated and addresses a genuine limitation of action-only conditioning (coarse global alignment). Rendering 2D condition maps and injecting them via a zero-initialized projector is a lightweight, sensible design.

The dataset curation pipeline is a substantial engineering effort (Monst3R + NKSR/voxelization for occupancy, GroundingDINO + SAM2 for instance tracking, Qwen-VL captioning + K-means for a dataset-level label set), and could be a useful community resource if actually released.

Quantitative results in Table 2 are consistently favorable across three datasets (e.g., BridgeV2 PSNR 28.26 vs 25.28 for IRASim, FID 3.42 vs 8.85), and the ablations in Tables 3–4 show that added conditioning and pretraining help.

The extensions (ORV-MV for multi-view and ORV-S2R for sim-to-real) demonstrate ambition and breadth, and the supplementary provides reasonably detailed training/preprocessing hyperparameters (Table 6) and compute reporting.
weaknesses: The provenance of the occupancy condition maps at inference time is never specified, and it appears to risk ground-truth leakage. For the real-data experiments (Table 2, Figure 6), the model predicts 15 future frames from a one-frame observation, yet Figure 4's inference path routes 4D Reconstruction through a Gaussian renderer to produce the condition maps. A single observation frame cannot yield a 16-frame 4D occupancy; the curation pipeline (Sec. 3.1) reconstructs occupancy from the full raw video via Monst3R. If the conditioning sequence is derived from the ground-truth video being predicted, then the comparison against action-only baselines (IRASim, HMA, AVID) is invalid and the headline results are not meaningful. This is the single most consequential issue and must be clarified explicitly.

The comparison confounds the representation with the information. Table 3 (base 25.63 → full cond 28.26) measures the gain from adding a dense, pixel-aligned visual condition, not from the occupancy representation per se. The authors themselves note that ControlNet-like conditioning offers 'stronger and more refined pixel-level control,' yet no such dense-conditioning baseline is trained and compared, so the claim that occupancy specifically matters is unestablished.

No downstream evaluation, despite the framing. The abstract/introduction motivate the work through robot learning, imitation learning, and policy learning, and multi-view generation is justified because it 'can largely help with robot learning'—yet no policy-learning, imitation-learning, or success-rate experiment is reported. Only perceptual metrics (PSNR/SSIM/FID/FVD) are provided.

The sim-to-real claim (Sec. 3.4, Figure 7) rests on a single qualitative example. The assertion of 'higher efficiency than original physical simulators' is unquantified, and no policy-transfer or task-success measurement is given.

Multi-view results are qualitative only (Figure 8), with no multi-view consistency metric (e.g., reprojection error or multi-view FVD); the paper concedes a color/lighting discrepancy in the generated views.

The baseline set is thin and the comparison table is incomplete. Only IRASim, HMA, AVID, and CogVideoX are compared, with many cells marked '—'; several recent, directly relevant methods cited in related work (e.g., RoboTransfer, Gen2Act, This&That, Ctrl-World, UniSim) are not compared. It is also unclear whether baselines were retrained under identical data/compute or numbers were copied from prior papers.

Methodological novelty is limited and largely compositional. The core mechanism is a soft dense visual condition (acknowledged as a weaker analogue of ControlNet) applied to a pretrained CogVideoX-2B; the new element is the construction of the conditioning signal, which itself relies on off-the-shelf components (Monst3R, NKSR, GroundingDINO, SAM2, Qwen-VL).

Ablations are incomplete: there is no study of voxel/occupancy resolution, number of condition frames, or sensitivity to occupancy-prediction error. The 'w/ depth' and 'w/ sem' reconstruction-vs-rendering numbers are close and their interpretation is vague, weakening the practical-applicability claim.

Evaluation metrics are weak for generative fidelity: PSNR/SSIM (the authors themselves cite PSNR's limited validity [110]) plus FID/FVD on ~2.6K samples, which the paper acknowledges is a small sample for FVD.

Presentation and consistency issues: the abstract ends with a dangling 'Demo, Code & Model:'; the text cites 'Table 7' for the pretraining ablation while Table 7 is the multi-view sample-proportion table (the intended reference is Table 4); and the code/model/data links are truncated, leaving reproducibility claims unverifiable.
